title: Given a binary tree and a target sum, determine whether the tree has any root-to-leaf path such that adding up all the node values along the path equals the target sum. Return true or false, and explain why a depth-first traversal is the natural fit for this problem.
shortTitle: Binary Tree Path Sum (Does a Root-to-Leaf Path Equal a Target?)

s1_definition.oneliner: Walk each root-to-leaf path depth-first, subtract each node's value from the target, and return true when a leaf makes the remainder exactly zero.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Tree DFS pattern** – recursively walk from root to each leaf, tracking the running target.
- **Subtract as you go** – at each node, subtract the node's value from the remaining target.
- **Leaf test** – success occurs only at a true leaf (both children null) where the remaining target equals zero.
- **Short-circuit** – combine left and right results with logical OR; the search stops at the first valid path.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time (visits each node once), O(h) space for the recursion stack.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh submits a request that flows down a chain of approval desks. Each desk charges a processing fee. The budget is the target sum, and you need to know if any complete top-to-bottom chain of fees adds up to exactly the budget. You follow one chain all the way down, subtracting each fee, and check if the budget hits zero at the final desk.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Tree:            Target = 800
       500
      /   \
    200   300
   /   \
  100   150

  DFS Trace (subtract as you go):
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ hasPathSum(500, 800)                         │
  │   remaining = 800 - 500 = 300                │
  │   Not a leaf, recurse:                       │
  │                                              │
  │   hasPathSum(200, 300)                       │
  │     remaining = 300 - 200 = 100              │
  │     Not a leaf, recurse:                     │
  │                                              │
  │     hasPathSum(100, 100)                     │
  │       remaining = 100 - 100 = 0              │
  │       LEAF! remaining == 0 -> return TRUE    │
  │                                              │
  │   Left child returned true, short-circuit    │
  │   (right child 300 not explored)             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Leaf Test (correctness):
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ A LEAF has both children null.               │
  │ A NULL child is NOT a leaf.                  │
  │ Check at leaf, not at null, to avoid         │
  │ false positives from single-child nodes.     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Binary Tree Path Sum is the classic Tree Depth First Search problem. You walk from the root to each leaf, subtracting each node's value from the running target. At a leaf, you check whether the remaining target is exactly zero. For non-leaf nodes, you combine the left and right results with logical OR, short-circuiting as soon as one valid path is found.

The most important correctness detail is the leaf test. You only declare success at a true leaf where both children are null, never at a null child. Checking at null creates false positives when a single-child node's missing child happens to make the remaining target zero. This is the bug interviewers are watching for.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this pattern to validate approval fee chains. A transfer request flowed through a tree of approval desks, each charging a BigDecimal fee, and compliance needed to confirm that at least one complete chain carried fees summing to exactly the budgeted amount. Using BigDecimal's compareTo for the zero check ensured money-safe comparison.

The senior depth comes from knowing the Path Sum family: Path Sum I (this problem), Path Sum II (collect all valid paths via backtracking), Path Sum III (count paths from any node using prefix sums), and Max Path Sum (global maximum with DFS). Understanding the full family shows mastery of tree DFS.

Remember one sentence: Subtract each node's value from the target as you descend, and declare success only at a true leaf where the remaining target hits exactly zero.

---

keyPoints: Subtract each node's value from the target as you descend; check for zero at leaves.
Leaf test: both children must be null; checking at null causes false positives.
Combine left and right with logical OR for short-circuit on the first valid path.
Time O(n), space O(h) for the recursion stack.
With negative node values, you cannot prune early; must always reach a leaf.
Part of the Path Sum family: I (boolean), II (all paths), III (any-node start), Max (global max).
